learn.title: Following the address
learn.body: A pointer holds an address. To reach the value stored there, you dereference it with the star: `*p`. The expression `*p` means the thing `p` points at. You can read it, and you can also assign to it.

learn.title: Read and write through p
learn.body: This prints 7, then 9, then `10 10`. Writing `*p = 9` changes `n` itself, because `p` points at `n`. The last line shows `n` and `*p` always agree.

learn.title: Tracing it
steps: `*p * 2` is 8, and it is stored where `p` points

learn.title: Three jobs for the star
learn.body: The star appears in three roles. In `a * b` it multiplies. In a declaration like `int *p` it marks a pointer. In an expression like `*p` it dereferences. Look at where it sits to tell which one it is.
`p` is the address. `*p` is the value at that address. `&n` goes the other way: from a value to its address.

questions.prompt: To read the value that `p` points at, write \_\_.
questions.explanation: The star in front of a pointer dereferences it.
Writing through `*p` changes the variable `p` points at.
`*p` is 4, doubled is 8, and it is stored in `n`.

questions.prompt: `int n = 7; int *p = &n; *p = *p + 1;` What does `printf("%d", n)` show?
questions.explanation: `*p + 1` is 8 and it is stored into n through the pointer.

questions.prompt: Which expression gives the address of `n`?
Match each expression to its meaning.
questions.explanation: A pointer is also a variable, so it has its own address.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order to change `n` through a pointer.
questions.explanation: The pointer needs something to point at before you write through it.
